PyTorch GRU uses reset-after-linear: split input and recurrent affine outputs in gate order `(r,z,n)`; compute `r=sigmoid(ir+hr)`, `z=sigmoid(iz+hz)`, `n=tanh(inn+r*hn)`, then `h=(1-z)*n+z*h_prev`. The reset multiplies the recurrent candidate bias too. Applying reset before the recurrent matrix changes the model. Built-in dropout acts between stacked GRU layers, excluding the final layer; a single-layer GRU has no internal dropout. [Official GRU documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/generated/torch.nn.GRU.html). Recommended equivalence check: copy all weights/biases, disable dropout, compare sequence outputs, final states, input/initial-state gradients and parameter gradients using identical upstream gradients. Allow floating-point tolerance for different kernels; mathematical equivalence does not guarantee bitwise equality.

Constructing `nn.Linear` consumes RNG through `reset_parameters()`, even if its weights are immediately zeroed. For an added CPU-created layer, construct and zero it inside `with torch.random.fork_rng(devices=[]):`; CPU RNG state is always saved and restored. For direct CUDA construction, include the relevant CUDA device ID. Zero both weight and bias where present. This preserves the surrounding PyTorch RNG stream without reseeding; it does not preserve Python/NumPy RNG or cancel randomness subsequently used by the new forward path. Keep baseline module construction order unchanged. [Linear implementation](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/torch/nn/modules/linear.py), [fork_rng documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/random.html).
